entries.2d5ff5cda5c7338bdfed6cacf3f8c0b50204cc35: <div sID="gen2988" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Num.16" sID="Num.16"/> <div eID="gen2988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2990" type="x-p"/> The date of the history contained in this chapter is altogether uncertain. Probably these mutinies happened after their removal back again from Kadesh-barnea, when they were fixed (if I may so speak) for their wandering in the wilderness, and began to look upon that as their settlement. Presently after new laws given follows the story of a new rebellion, as if sin took occasion from the commandment to become more exceedingly sinful. Here is, I. A daring and dangerous rebellion raised against Moses and Aaron, by Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, <reference osisRef="Num.16.1-Num.16.15">ver. 1-15</reference>. 1. Korah and his accomplices contend for the priesthood against Aaron, <reference osisRef="Num.16.3">ver. 3</reference>. Moses reasons with them, and appeals to God for a decision of the controversy, <reference osisRef="Num.16.4-Num.16.11">ver. 4-11</reference>. 2. Dathan and Abiram quarrel with Moses, and refuse to obey his summons, which greatly grieves him, <reference osisRef="Num.16.12-Num.16.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. II. A solemn appearance of the pretenders to the priesthood before God, according to order, and a public appearance of the glory of the Lord, which would have consumed the whole congregation if Moses and Aaron had not interceded, <reference osisRef="Num.16.16-Num.16.22">ver. 16-22</reference>. III. The deciding of the controversy, and the crushing of the rebellion, by the cutting off of the rebels. 1. Those in their tents were buried alive, <reference osisRef="Num.16.23-Num.16.34">ver. 23-34</reference>. 2. Those at the door of the tabernacle were consumed by fire (<reference osisRef="Num.16.35">ver. 35</reference>), and their censers preserved for a memorial, <reference osisRef="Num.16.37-Num.16.40">ver. 37-40</reference>. IV. A new insurrection of the people, <reference osisRef="Num.16.41-Num.16.43">ver. 41-43</reference>. 1. God stayed in the insurrection by a plague, <reference osisRef="Num.16.45">ver. 45</reference>. 2. Aaron stayed the plague by offering incense, <reference osisRef="Num.16.46-Num.16.50">ver. 46-50</reference>. The manner and method of recording this story plainly show the ferment to have been very great.
entries.666a5edce7b3ec5a3963bd74e4f7d06ab111c662: <div eID="gen2990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2989" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took <hi type="italic">men:</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> And they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown: <hi type="super">3</hi> And they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said unto them, <hi type="italic">Ye take</hi> too much upon you, seeing all the congregation <hi type="italic">are</hi> holy, every one of them, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> among them: wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">4</hi> And when Moses heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he fell upon his face: <hi type="super">5</hi> And he spake unto Korah and unto all his company, saying, Even to morrow the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will show who <hi type="italic">are</hi> his, and <hi type="italic">who is</hi> holy; and will cause <hi type="italic">him</hi> to come near unto him: even <hi type="italic">him</hi> whom he hath chosen will he cause to come near unto him. 6 This do; Take you censers, Korah, and all his company; 7 And put fire therein, and put incense in them before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to morrow: and it shall be <hi type="italic">that</hi> the man whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> doth choose, he <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> holy: <hi type="italic">ye take</hi> too much upon you, ye sons of Levi. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Moses said unto Korah, Hear, I pray you, ye sons of Levi: <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Seemeth it but</hi> a small thing unto you, that the God of Israel hath separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself to do the service of the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to stand before the congregation to minister unto them? <hi type="super">10</hi> And he hath brought thee near <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> and all thy brethren the sons of Levi with thee: and seek ye the priesthood also? <hi type="super">11</hi> For which cause <hi type="italic">both</hi> thou and all thy company <hi type="italic">are</hi> gathered together against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> Aaron, that ye murmur against him? <div eID="gen2991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2992" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An account of the rebels, who and what they were, not, as formerly, the mixed multitude and the dregs of the people, who are therefore never named, but men of distinction and quality, that made a figure. Korah was the ring-leader: he formed and headed the faction; therefore it is called <hi type="italic">the gainsaying of Korah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.11">Jude 11</reference>. He was cousin-german to Moses, they were brothers' children, yet the nearness of the relation could not restrain him from being insolent and rude to Moses. Think it not strange if a man's foes be <hi type="italic">those of his own house.</hi> With him joined Dathan and Abiram, chief men of the tribe of Reuben, the eldest son of Jacob. Probably Korah was disgusted both at the preferment of Aaron to the priesthood and the constituting of Elizaphan to the head of the Kohathites (<reference osisRef="Num.3.30">ch. iii. 30</reference>); and perhaps the Reubenites were angry that the tribe of Judah had the first post of honour in the camp. <hi type="italic">On</hi> is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Num.16.1">v. 1</reference>) as one of the heads of the faction, but never after in the whole story, either because, as some think, he repented and left them, or because he did not make himself so remarkable as Dathan and Abiram did. The Kohathites encamped on the same side of the tabernacle that the Reubenites did, which perhaps gave Korah an opportunity of drawing them in, whence the Jews say, <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked man, and woe to his neighbour,</hi> who is in danger of being infected by him. And, these being themselves <hi type="italic">men of renown,</hi> they seduced into the conspiracy <hi type="italic">two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.2">v. 2</reference>); probably they were first-born, or at least heads of families, who, before the elevation of Aaron, had themselves ministered in holy things. Note, The pride, ambition, and emulation, of great men, have always been the occasion of a great deal of mischief both in churches and states. God by his grace make great men humble, and so give peace in our time, O Lord! Famous men, and men of renown, as these are described to be, were the great sinners of the old world, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Gen. vi. 4</reference>. The fame and renown which they had did not content them; they were high, but would be higher, and thus the famous men became infamous. <div eID="gen2992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2993" type="x-p"/> II. The rebels' remonstrance, <reference osisRef="Num.16.3">v. 3</reference>. That which they quarrel with is the settlement of the priesthood upon Aaron and his family, which they think an honour too great for Moses to give and Aaron to accept, and so they are both charged with usurpation: <hi type="italic">You take too much upon you;</hi> or, "Let it suffice you to have domineered thus long, and now think of resigning your places to those who have as good a title to them and are as well able to manage them." 1. They proudly boast of the holiness of the congregation, and the presence of God in it. "They are <hi type="italic">holy, every one of them,</hi> and as fit to be employed in offering sacrifice as Aaron is, and as masters of families formerly were, and <hi type="italic">the Lord is among them,</hi> to direct and own them." Small reason they had to boast of the people's purity, or of God's favour, as the people had been so frequently and so lately polluted with sin, and were now under the marks of God's displeasure, which should have made them thankful for priests to mediate between them and God; but, instead of that, they envy them. 2. They unjustly charge Moses and Aaron with taking the honour they had to themselves, whereas it was evident, beyond contradiction, that they were called of God to it, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">Heb. v. 4</reference>. So that they would either have no priests at all, nor any government, none to preside either in civil or sacred things, none over the congregation, none above it, or they would not acquiesce in that constitution of the government which God had appointed. See here, (1.) What spirit levellers are of, and those that despise dominions, and resist the powers that God has set over them; they are proud, envious, ambitious, turbulent, wicked, and unreasonable men. (2.) What usage even the best and most useful men may expect, even from those they have been serviceable to. If those be represented as usurpers that have the best titles, and those as tyrants that govern best, let them recollect that Moses and Aaron were thus abused. <div eID="gen2993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2994" type="x-p"/> III. Moses's conduct when their remonstrance was published against him. How did he take it? <div eID="gen2994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2995" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">fell on his face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.4">v. 4</reference>), as before, <reference osisRef="Num.14.5">ch. xiv. 5</reference>. Thus he showed how willing he would have been to yield to them, and how gladly he would have resigned his government, if it would have consisted with his duty to God and his fidelity to the trust reposed in him. Thus also he applied to God, by prayer, for direction what to say and to do upon this sad occasion. He would not speak to them till he had thus humbled and composed his own spirit (which could not but begin to be heated), and had received instruction from God. The <hi type="italic">heart of the wise</hi> in such a case <hi type="italic">studies to answer,</hi> and asks counsel at God's mouth. <div eID="gen2995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2996" type="x-p"/> 2. He agrees to refer the case to God, and leave it to him to decide it, as one well assured of the goodness of his title, and yet well content to resign, if God thought fit, to gratify this discontented people with another nomination. An honest cause fears not a speedy trial; even to-morrow let it be brought on, <reference osisRef="Num.16.5-Num.16.7">v. 5-7</reference>. Let Korah and his partisans bring their censers, and offer incense before the Lord, and, if he testify his acceptance of them, well and good; Moses is now as willing that all the Lord's people should be priests, if God so pleased, as before that they should all be prophets, <reference osisRef="Num.11.29">ch. xi. 29</reference>. But if God, upon an appeal to him, determine (as no doubt he would) for Aaron, they would find it highly dangerous to make the experiment: and therefore he puts it off till to-morrow, to try whether, when they had slept upon it, they would desist, and let fall their pretensions. <div eID="gen2996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2997" type="x-p"/> 3. He argues the case fairly with them, to still the mutiny with fair reasoning, if possible, before the appeal came to God's tribunal, for then he knew it would end in the confusion of the complainants. <div eID="gen2997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2998" type="x-p"/> (1.) He calls them <hi type="italic">the sons of Levi,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.7">v. 7</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Num.16.8">v. 8</reference>. They were of his own tribe, nay, they were of God's tribe; it was therefore the worse in them thus to mutiny both against God and against him. It was not long since the sons of Levi had bravely appeared on God's side, in the matter of the golden calf, and got immortal honour by it; and shall those that were then the only innocents now be the leading criminals, and lose all the honour they had won? Could there be such chaff on God's floor? Levites, and yet rebels? <div eID="gen2998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2999" type="x-p"/> (2.) He retorts their charge upon themselves. They had unjustly charged Moses and Aaron with taking too much upon them, though they had done no more than what God put upon them; nay, says Moses, <hi type="italic">You take too much upon you, you sons of Levi.</hi> Note, Those that take upon them to control and contradict God's appointment take too much upon them. It is enough for us to submit; it is too much to prescribe. <div eID="gen2999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3000" type="x-p"/> (3.) He shows them the privilege they had as Levites, which was sufficient for them, they needed not to aspire to the honour of the priesthood, <reference osisRef="Num.16.9-Num.16.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. He reminds them how great the honour was to which they were preferred, as Levites. [1.] They were <hi type="italic">separated from the congregation of Israel,</hi> distinguished from them, dignified above them; instead of complaining that Aaron's family was advanced above theirs, they ought to have been thankful that their tribe was advanced above the rest of the tribes, though they had been in all respects upon the level with them. Note, It will help to keep us from envying those that are above us duly to consider how many there are below us. Instead of fretting that any are preferred before us in honour, power, estate, or interest, in gifts, graces, or usefulness, we have reason to bless God if we, who are less than the least, are not put among the very last. Many perhaps who deserve better are not preferred so well. [2.] They were separated to very great and valuable honours, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To <hi type="italic">draw near to God,</hi> nearer than the common Israelites, though they also were a people near unto him; the nearer any are to God the greater is their honour. <hi type="italic">Secondly, To do the service of the tabernacle.</hi> It is honour enough to bear the vessels of the sanctuary, and to be employed in any part of the service of the tabernacle. God's service is not only perfect freedom, but high preferment. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> To <hi type="italic">stand before the congregation to minister unto them.</hi> Note, Those are truly great that serve the public, and it is the honour of God's ministers to be the church's ministers; nay, which adds to the dignity put upon them, [3.] It was the God of Israel himself that separated them. It was his act and deed to put them into their place, and therefore they ought not to have been discontented: and he it was likewise that put Aaron into his place, and therefore they ought not to have envied him. <div eID="gen3000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3001" type="x-p"/> (4.) He convicts them of the sin of undervaluing those privileges: <hi type="italic">Seemeth it a small thing unto you?</hi> As if he had said, "It ill becomes you of all men to grudge Aaron the priesthood, when at the same time that he was advanced to that honour you were designed for another honour dependent upon it, and shine with rays borrowed from him." Note, [1.] The privilege of drawing near to the God of Israel is not a small thing in itself, and therefore must not appear small to us. To those who neglect opportunities of drawing near to God, who are careless and formal in it, to whom it is a task and not a pleasure, we may properly put this question: "Seemeth it a small thing to you that God has made you a people near unto him?" [2.] Those who aspire after and usurp the honours forbidden them put a great contempt upon the honours allowed them. We have each of us as good a share of reputation as God sees fit for us, and sees us fit for, and much better than we deserve; and we ought to rest satisfied with it, and not, as these, <hi type="italic">exercise ourselves in things too high for us: Seek you the priesthood also?</hi> They would not <hi type="italic">own</hi> that they sought it, but Moses saw that they had this in their eye; the law had provided very well for those that served at the altar, and therefore they would put in for the office. <div eID="gen3001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3002" type="x-p"/> (5.) He interprets their mutiny to be a rebellion against God (<reference osisRef="Num.16.11">v. 11</reference>); while they pretended to assert the holiness and liberty of the Israel of God, they really took up arms against the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">You are gathered together against the Lord.</hi> Note, Those that strive against God's ordinances and providences, whatever they pretend, and whether they are aware of it or no, do indeed strive with their Maker. Those resist the prince who resist those that are commissioned by him: for, alas! says Moses, <hi type="italic">What is Aaron, that you murmur against him?</hi> If murmurers and complainers would consider that the instruments they quarrel with are but instruments whom God employs, and that they are but what he makes them, and neither more nor less, better nor worse, they would not be so bold and free in their censures and reproaches as they are. Those that found the priesthood, as it was settled, a blessing, must give all the praise to God; but if any found it a burden they must not therefore quarrel with Aaron, who is but what he is made, and does but as he is bidden. Thus he interested God in the cause, and so might be sure of speeding well in his appeal.
entries.b5fdd9f55ee590c64ce142081ff46592a259d9d0: <div eID="gen3002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab: which said, We will not come up: <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> a small thing that thou hast brought us up out of a land that floweth with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, except thou make thyself altogether a prince over us? <hi type="super">14</hi> Moreover thou hast not brought us into a land that floweth with milk and honey, or given us inheritance of fields and vineyards: wilt thou put out the eyes of these men? we will not come up. 15 And Moses was very wroth, and said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Respect not thou their offering: I have not taken one ass from them, neither have I hurt one of them. 16 And Moses said unto Korah, Be thou and all thy company before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou, and they, and Aaron, to morrow: <hi type="super">17</hi> And take every man his censer, and put incense in them, and bring ye before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> every man his censer, two hundred and fifty censers; thou also, and Aaron, each <hi type="italic">of you</hi> his censer. 18 And they took every man his censer, and put fire in them, and laid incense thereon, and stood in the door of the tabernacle of the congregation with Moses and Aaron. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Korah gathered all the congregation against them unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation: and the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> appeared unto all the congregation. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment. <hi type="super">22</hi> And they fell upon their faces, and said, O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation? <div eID="gen3003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The insolence of Dathan and Abiram, and their treasonable remonstrance. Moses had heard what Korah had to say, and had answered it; now he summons Dathan and Abiram to bring in their complaints (<reference osisRef="Num.16.12">v. 12</reference>); but they would not obey his summons, either because they could not for shame say that to his face which they were resolved to say, and then it is an instance of some remains of modesty in them; or, rather, because they would not so far own his authority, and then it is an instance of the highest degree of impudence. They spoke the language of Pharaoh himself, who set Moses at defiance, but they forgot how dearly he paid for it. Had not their heads been wretchedly heated, and their hearts hardened, they might have considered that, if they regarded not these messengers, Moses could soon in God's name send messengers of death for them. But thus the God of this world <hi type="italic">blinds the minds of those that believe not.</hi> But by the same messengers they send their articles of impeachment against Moses; and the charge runs very high. 1. They charge him with having done them a great deal of wrong in bringing them out of Egypt, invidiously calling that <hi type="italic">a land flowing with milk and honey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.13">v. 13</reference>. Onions, and garlick, and fish, they had indeed plenty of in Egypt, but it never pretended to milk and honey; only they would thus banter the promise of Canaan. Ungrateful wretches, to represent that as an injury to them which was really the greatest favour that ever was bestowed upon any people! 2. They charge him with a design upon their lives, that he intended to <hi type="italic">kill them in the wilderness,</hi> though they were so well provided for. And, if they were sentenced to die in the wilderness, they must thank themselves. Moses would have healed them, and they would not be healed. 3. They charge him with a design upon their liberties, that he meant to enslave them, by <hi type="italic">making himself a prince over them.</hi> A prince over them! Was he not a tender father to them? nay, their devoted servant for the Lord's sake? Had they not their properties secured, their order preserved, and justice impartially administered? Did they not live in ease and honour? And yet they complain as if Moses's yoke were heavier than Pharaoh's. And did Moses make himself a prince? Far from it. How gladly would he have declined the office at first! How gladly would he have resigned it many a time since! And yet he is thus put under the blackest characters of a tyrant and a usurper. 4. They charge him with cheating them, raising their expectations of a good land, and then defeating them (<reference osisRef="Num.16.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast not brought us,</hi> as thou promisedst us, <hi type="italic">into a land that floweth with milk and honey;</hi> and pray whose fault was that? He had brought them to the borders of it, and was just ready, under God, to put them in possession of it; but they thrust it away from them, and shut the door against themselves; so that it was purely their own fault that they were not now in Canaan, and yet Moses must bear the blame. Thus when the <hi type="italic">foolishness of man perverteth his way his heart fretteth against the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Prov. xix. 3</reference>. 5. They charge him in the general with unfair dealing, that he put <hi type="italic">out the eyes of these men,</hi> and then meant to lead them blindfold as he pleased. The design of all he did for them was to open their eyes, and yet they insinuate that he intended to put out their eyes, that they might not see themselves imposed upon. Note, The wisest and best cannot please everybody, nor gain the good word of all. Those often fall under the heaviest censures who have merited the highest applause. Many a good work Moses had shown them from the Father, and for which of these do they reproach him? <div eID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> II. Moses's just resentment of their insolence, <reference osisRef="Num.16.15">v. 15</reference>. Moses, though the meekest man, yet, finding God reproached in him, <hi type="italic">was very wroth;</hi> he could not bear to see a people ruining themselves for whose salvation he had done so much. In this discomposure, <div eID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3006" type="x-p"/> 1. He appeals to God concerning his own integrity; whereas they basely reflected upon him as ambitious, covetous, and oppressive, in making himself a prince over them, God was his witness, (1.) That he never got any thing by them: <hi type="italic">I have not taken one ass from them,</hi> not only not by way of bribery and extortion, but not by way of recompence or gratuity for all the good offices he had done them; he never took the pay of a general, or the salary of a judge, much less the tribute of a prince. He got more in his estate when he kept Jethro's flock than when he came to be king in Jeshurun. (2.) That they never lost any thing by him: <hi type="italic">Neither have I hurt any one of them,</hi> no, not the least, no, not the worst, no, not those that had been most peevish and provoking to him: he never abused his power to the support of wrong. Note, Those that have never blemished themselves need not fear being slurred by others: when men condemn us we may be easy, if our own hearts condemn us not. <div eID="gen3006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> 2. He begs of God to plead his cause, and clear him, by showing his displeasure at the incense which Korah and his company were to offer, with whom Dathan and Abiram were in confederacy. Lord, says he, <hi type="italic">Respect not thou their offering.</hi> Herein he seems to refer to the history of Cain, lately written by his own hand, of whom it is said that to him and his offering God had not respect, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.5">Gen. iv. 5</reference>. These that <hi type="italic">followed the gainsaying of Korah walked in the way of Cain</hi> (these are put together, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.11">Jude 11</reference>), and therefore he prays that they might be frowned upon as Cain was, and put to the same confusion. <div eID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> III. Issue joined between Moses and his accusers. 1. Moses challenges them to appear with Aaron next morning, at the time of offering up the morning incense, and refer the matter to God's judgment, <reference osisRef="Num.16.16-Num.16.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Since he could not convince them by his calm and affectionate reasoning, he is ready to enter into bonds to stand God's award, not doubting but that God would appear, to decide the controversy. This reference he had agreed to before (<reference osisRef="Num.16.6-Num.16.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), and here adds only one clause, which bespeaks his great condescension to the plaintiffs, that Aaron, against whose advancement they excepted, though now advanced by the divine institution to the honour of burning incense within the tabernacle, yet, upon this trial, should put himself into the place of a probationer, and stand upon the level with Korah, at the door of the tabernacle; nay, and Moses himself would stand with them, so that the complainant shall have all the fair dealing he can desire; and thus <hi type="italic">every mouth shall be stopped.</hi> 2. Korah accepts the challenge, and makes his appearance with Moses and Aaron <hi type="italic">at the door of the tabernacle,</hi> to make good his pretensions, <reference osisRef="Num.16.18-Num.16.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. If he had not had a very great stock of impudence, he could not have carried on the matter thus far. Had not he lately seen Nadab and Abihu, the consecrated priests, struck dead for daring to offer incense with unhallowed fire? and could he and his accomplices expect to fare any better in offering incense with unhallowed hands? Yet, to confront Moses and Aaron, in the height of his pride he thus bids defiance to Heaven, and pretends to demand the divine acceptance without a divine warrant; thus wretchedly is the heart hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. They <hi type="italic">took every man his censer.</hi> Perhaps these were some of the censers which these heads of families had made use of at their family-altars, before this part of religious service was confined to the priesthood and the altar in the tabernacle (and they would bring them into use and reputation again); or they might be common chafing-dishes, which were for their ordinary use. Now to attend the solemn trial, and to be witness of the issue, one would have thought Moses should have <hi type="italic">gathered the congregation against the rebels,</hi> but it seems Korah gathered them against Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.16.19">v. 19</reference>), which intimates that a great part of the congregation sided with Korah, were at his beck, and wished him success, and that Korah's hopes were very high of carrying the point against Aaron; for, had he suspected the event, he would not have coveted to make the trial thus public: but little did he think that he was now calling the congregation together to be the witnesses of his own confusion! Note, Proud and ambitious men, while they are projecting their own advancement, often prove to have been hurrying on their own shameful fall. <div eID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> IV. The judgment set, and the Judge taking the tribunal, and threatening to give sentence against the whole congregation. 1. The <hi type="italic">glory of the Lord appeared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.19">v. 19</reference>. The same glory that appeared to instal Aaron in his office at first (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.23">Lev. ix. 23</reference>) now appeared to confirm him in it, and to confound those that oppose him, and set up themselves in competition with him. The <hi type="italic">Shechinah,</hi> or divine Majesty, the glory of the eternal Word, which ordinarily dwelt between the cherubim within the veil, now was publicly seen over the door of the tabernacle, to the terror of the whole congregation; for, though they saw no manner of similitude, yet probably the appearances of the light and fire were such as plainly showed God to be angry with them; as when he appeared, <reference osisRef="Num.14.10">ch. xiv. 10</reference>. Nothing is more terrible to those who are conscious of guilt than the appearances of divine glory; for such a glorious Being must needs be a formidable enemy. 2. God threatened to <hi type="italic">consume them all in a moment,</hi> and, in order to that, bade Moses and Aaron stand from among them, <reference osisRef="Num.16.21">v. 21</reference>. God thus showed what their sin deserved, and how very provoking it was to him. See what a dangerous thing it is to have fellowship with sinners, and in the least to partake with them. Many of the congregation, it is likely, came only for company, following the crowd, or for curiosity, to see the issue, yet not coming, as they ought to have done, to bear their testimony against the rebels, and openly to declare for God and Moses, they had like to have been all consumed in a moment. If we follow the herd into which the devil has entered, it is at our peril. <div eID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> V. The humble intercession of Moses and Aaron for the congregation, <reference osisRef="Num.16.22">v. 22</reference>. 1. Their posture was importuning: they <hi type="italic">fell on their faces,</hi> prostrating themselves before God, as supplicants in good earnest, that they might prevail for sparing mercy. Though the people had treacherously deserted them, and struck in with those that were in arms against them, yet they approved themselves faithful to the trusts reposed in them, as shepherds of Israel, who were to stand in the breach when they saw the flock in danger. Note, If others fail in their duty to us, this does not discharge us from our duty to them, nor take off the obligations we lie under to seek their welfare. 2. Their prayer was a pleading prayer, and it proved a prevailing one. Now God would have <hi type="italic">destroyed them</hi> if Moses had not <hi type="italic">turned away his wrath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Ps. cvi. 23</reference>); yet far be it from us to imagine that Moses was more considerate or more compassionate than God in such a case as this: but God saw fit to show his just displeasure against the sin of sinners by the sentence, and at the same time to show his gracious condescension to the prayers of the saints, by the revocation of the sentence at the intercession of Moses. Observe in the prayer, (1.) The title they give to God: <hi type="italic">The God of the spirits of all flesh.</hi> See what man is; he is a spirit in flesh, a soul embodied, a creature wonderfully compounded of heaven and earth. See what God is; he is the God of the spirits of all mankind. <hi type="italic">He forms the spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.1">Zech. xii. 1</reference>. He <hi type="italic">fathers it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.9">Heb. xii. 9</reference>. He has an ability to fashion it (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.15">Ps. xxxiii. 15</reference>), and authority to dispose of it, for he has said, <hi type="italic">All souls are mine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.4">Ezek. xviii. 4</reference>. They insinuate hereby that though, as <hi type="italic">the God of the spirits of all flesh,</hi> he might in sovereignty consume this congregation in a moment, yet it was to be hoped that he would in mercy spare them, not only because they were the work of his own hands, and he had a propriety in them, but because, being the <hi type="italic">God of spirits,</hi> he knew their frame, and could distinguish between the leaders and the led, between those who sinned maliciously and those who were drawn in by their wiles, and would make a difference accordingly in his judgments. (2.) The argument they insist on; it is much the same with that which Abraham urged in his intercession for Sodom (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.23">Gen. xviii. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wilt thou destroy the righteous with the wicked?</hi> Such is the plea here: <hi type="italic">Shall one man sin and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation?</hi> Not but that it was the sin of them all to join in this matter, but the great transgression was his that first hatched the treason. Note, Whatever God may do in sovereignty and strict justice, we have reason to hope that he will not destroy a congregation for the sin of one, but that, <hi type="italic">righteousness and peace</hi> having <hi type="italic">kissed each other</hi> in the undertaking of the Redeemer, <hi type="italic">mercy shall rejoice against judgment.</hi> Moses knew that all the congregation must perish in the wilderness by degrees, yet he is thus earnest in prayer that they might not be consumed at once, and would reckon it a favour to obtain a reprieve. <hi type="italic">Lord, let it alone this year.</hi>
entries.9fc244fbd0aacab55629b16fca46c18c213ac0e2: <div eID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">24</hi> Speak unto the congregation, saying, Get you up from about the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Moses rose up and went unto Dathan and Abiram; and the elders of Israel followed him. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he spake unto the congregation, saying, Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest ye be consumed in all their sins. <hi type="super">27</hi> So they gat up from the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, on every side: and Dathan and Abiram came out, and stood in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Moses said, Hereby ye shall know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sent me to do all these works; for <hi type="italic">I have</hi> not <hi type="italic">done them</hi> of mine own mind. <hi type="super">29</hi> If these men die the common death of all men, or if they be visited after the visitation of all men; <hi type="italic">then</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not sent me. <hi type="super">30</hi> But if the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> make a new thing, and the earth open her mouth, and swallow them up, with all that <hi type="italic">appertain</hi> unto them, and they go down quick into the pit; then ye shall understand that these men have provoked the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> And it came to pass, as he had made an end of speaking all these words, that the ground clave asunder that <hi type="italic">was</hi> under them: <hi type="super">32</hi> And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their houses, and all the men that <hi type="italic">appertained</hi> unto Korah, and all <hi type="italic">their</hi> goods. 33 They, and all that <hi type="italic">appertained</hi> to them, went down alive into the pit, and the earth closed upon them: and they perished from among the congregation. <hi type="super">34</hi> And all Israel that <hi type="italic">were</hi> round about them fled at the cry of them: for they said, Lest the earth swallow us up <hi type="italic">also.</hi> <div eID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3012" type="x-p"/> We have here the determining of the controversy with Dathan and Abiram, who rebelled against Moses, as in the next paragraph the determining of the controversy with Korah and his company, who would be rivals with Aaron. It should seem that Dathan and Abiram had set up a spacious tabernacle in the midst of the tents of their families, where they kept court, met in council, and hung out their flag of defiance against Moses; it is here called <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.27">27</reference>. There, as in the place of rendezvous, Dathan and Abiram staid, when Korah and his friends went up to the tabernacle of the Lord, waiting the issue of their trial; but here we are told how they had their business done, before that trial was over. For God will take what method he pleases in his judgments. <div eID="gen3012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3013" type="x-p"/> I. Public warning is given to the congregation to withdraw immediately from the tents of the rebels. 1. God bids Moses speak to this purport, <reference osisRef="Num.16.24">v. 24</reference>. This was in answer to Moses's prayer. He had begged that God would not <hi type="italic">destroy the whole congregation.</hi> "Well," says God, "I will not, provided they be so wise as to shift for their own safety, and get out of the way of danger. If they will quit the rebels, well and good, they shall not perish with them; otherwise, let them take what follows." Note, We cannot expect to reap benefit by the prayers of our friends for our salvation, unless we ourselves be diligent and faithful in making use of the means of salvation; for God never promised to save by miracles those that would not save themselves by means. Moses that had prayed for them must preach this to them, and warn them to <hi type="italic">flee from this wrath to come.</hi> 2. Moses accordingly repairs to the head-quarters of the rebels, leaving Aaron at the door of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Num.16.25">v. 25</reference>. Dathan and Abiram had contumaciously refused to come up to him (<reference osisRef="Num.16.12">v. 12</reference>), yet he humbly condescends to go down to them, to try if he could yet convince and reclaim them. Ministers must thus with meekness instruct those that oppose themselves, and not think it below them to stoop to those that are most stubborn, for their good. Christ himself stretches out his hand to a rebellious and gainsaying people. The seventy elders of Israel attend Moses and his guard, to secure him from the insolence of the rabble, and by their presence to put an honour upon him, and if possible to strike an awe upon the rebels. It is our duty to contribute all we can to the countenance and support of injured innocency and honour. 3. Proclamation is made that all manner of persons, as they tendered their own safety, should forthwith <hi type="italic">depart from the tents of these wicked men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.26">v. 26</reference>), and thus should signify that they deserted their cause and interest, detested their crimes and counsels, and dreaded the punishment coming upon them. Note, Those that would not perish with sinners must <hi type="italic">come out from among them,</hi> and be separate. In vain do we pray, <hi type="italic">Gather not our souls with sinners,</hi> if we save not ourselves from the <hi type="italic">untoward generation.</hi> God's people are called out of Babylon, lest they share both in her sins and in her plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen3013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3014" type="x-p"/> II. The congregation takes the warning, but the rebels themselves continue obstinate, <reference osisRef="Num.16.27">v. 27</reference>. 1. God, in mercy, inclined the people to forsake the rebels: <hi type="italic">They got up from the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram,</hi> both those whose lot it was to pitch near them (who doubtless with themselves removed their families, and all their effects) and those also who had come from all parts of their camp to see the issue. It was in answer to the prayer of Moses that God thus stirred up the hearts of the congregation to shift for their own preservation. Note, To those whom God will save he gives repentance, that they may <hi type="italic">recover themselves out of the snare of the devil.</hi> Grace to separate from evil doers is one of the things that accompany salvation. 2. God, in justice, left the rebels to the obstinacy and hardness of their own hearts. Though they saw themselves abandoned by all their neighbours, and set up as a mark to the arrows of God's justice, yet instead of falling down and humbling themselves before God and Moses, owning their crime and begging pardon, instead of fleeing and dispersing themselves to seek for shelter in the crowd, they impudently <hi type="italic">stood in the doors of their tents,</hi> as if they would out-face God himself, and dare him to his worst. Thus were their hearts hardened to their own destruction, and they were fearless when their case was most fearful. But what a pity was it that their little children, who were not capable of guilt or fear, should by the presumption of their parents be put in this audacious posture! Happy they who are taught betimes to bow before God, and not as those unhappy little ones to stand it out against him! <div eID="gen3014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3015" type="x-p"/> III. Sentence is solemnly pronounced upon them by Moses in the name of the Lord, and the decision of the controversy is put upon the execution of that sentence by the almighty power of God. Moses, by divine instinct and direction, when the eyes of all Israel were fastened upon him, waiting the event, moved with a just and holy indignation at the impudence of the rebels, boldly puts the whole matter to a surprising issue, <reference osisRef="Num.16.28-Num.16.30">v. 28-30</reference>. 1. If the rebels die a common death, he will be content to be called and counted an impostor; not only if they die a natural death, but if they die by any sort of judgment that has formerly been executed on other malefactors. "If they die by the plague, or by fire from heaven, or by the sword, then say, God has disowned Moses;" but, 2. "If the earth open and swallow them up" (a punishment without precedent), "then let all the house of Israel know assuredly that I am God's servant, sent by him, and employed for him, and that those that fight against me fight against him." The judgment itself would have been proof enough of God's displeasure against the rebels, and would have given all men to <hi type="italic">understand that they had provoked the Lord;</hi> but when it was thus solemnly foretold and appealed to by Moses beforehand, when there was not the least previous indication of it from without, the convincing evidence of it was much the stronger, and it was put beyond dispute that he was not only a servant but a favourite of Heaven, who was so intimately acquainted with the divine counsels, and could obtain such extraordinary appearances of the divine power in his vindication. <div eID="gen3015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3016" type="x-p"/> IV. Execution is immediately done. It appeared that God and his servant Moses understood one another very well; for, as soon as ever Moses had spoken the word, God did the work, the earth <hi type="italic">clave asunder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.31">v. 31</reference>), <hi type="italic">opened her mouth, and swallowed them all up,</hi> them and theirs (<reference osisRef="Num.16.32">v. 32</reference>), and then <hi type="italic">closed upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.33">v. 33</reference>. This judgment was, 1. Unparalleled. God, in it, <hi type="italic">created a new thing,</hi> did what he never did before; for he has many arrows in his quiver; and there are diversities of operations in wrath as well as mercy. Dathan and Abiram thought themselves safe because they were at a distance from the <hi type="italic">shechinah,</hi> whence the fire of the Lord had sometimes issued, <hi type="italic">qui procul &#224; Jove</hi> (they say) <hi type="italic">procul &#224; fulmine—he who is far from Jove is far from the thunderbolt.</hi> But God made them to know that he was not tied up to one way of punishing; the earth, when he pleases, shall serve his justice as effectually as the fire. 2. It was very terrible to the sinners themselves to go down alive into their own graves, to be dead and buried in an instant, to go down thus to the bars of the pit when they were in their <hi type="italic">full strength wholly at ease and quiet.</hi> 3. It was severe upon their poor children, who, for the greater terror of the judgment, and fuller indication of the divine wrath, perished as parts of their parents, in which, though we cannot particularly tell how bad they might be to deserve it or how good God might be otherwise to them to compensate it, yet of this we are sure in the general, that Infinite Justice did them no wrong. <hi type="italic">Far be it from God that he should do iniquity.</hi> 4. It was altogether miraculous. The cleaving of the earth was as wonderful, and as much above the power of nature, as the cleaving of the sea, and the closing of the earth again more so than the closing of the waters. God has all the creatures at his command, and can make any of them, when he pleases, instruments of his justice; nor will any of them be our friends if he be our enemy. God now confirmed to Israel what Moses had lately taught them in that prayer of his, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of thy anger?</hi> He has, when he pleases, <hi type="italic">strange punishments for the workers of iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.3">Job xxxi. 3</reference>. Let us therefore conclude, <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?</hi> 5. It was very significant. They <hi type="italic">set their mouths against the heavens,</hi> and <hi type="italic">their throat was an open sepulchre;</hi> justly therefore does the earth open her mouth upon them and swallow them up. They made a rent in the congregation; justly therefore is the earth rent under them. Presumptuous sinners, that hate to be reformed, are a burden to the earth, the whole creation groans under them, which here was signified by this, that the earth sunk under these rebels, as weary of bearing them and being under them. And, considering how the earth is still in like manner loaded with the weight of iniquity, we have reason to wonder that this was the only time it ever sunk under its load. 6. It was typical of the eternal ruin of sinners who die impenitent, who, perhaps in allusion to this, are said to <hi type="italic">sink down into the pit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Ps. ix. 15</reference>) and to <hi type="italic">go down quickly into hell,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Ps. lv. 15</reference>. But David, even when he <hi type="italic">sinks in deep mire,</hi> yet prays in faith, <hi type="italic">Let not the pit shut her mouth upon me,</hi> as it does on the damned, between whom and life there is a gulf fixed, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.2-Ps.69.15">Ps. lxix. 2-15</reference>. His case was bad, but not, like this, desperate. <div eID="gen3016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3017" type="x-p"/> V. All Israel is alarmed at the judgment: <hi type="italic">They fled at the cry of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.34">v. 34</reference>. They cried for help when it was too late. Their doleful shrieks, instead of fetching their neighbours in to their relief, drove them so much the further off; for knowing their own guilt, and one another's, they hastened one another, saying, <hi type="italic">Lest the earth swallow us up also.</hi> Note, Others' ruins should be our warnings. Could we by faith hear the outcries of those that have gone down to the bottomless pit, we should give more diligence than we do to escape for our lives, lest we also come into that condemnation.
entries.f7bb811ffa68c79d563e7339be5dd30a633c1d5f: <div eID="gen3017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3018" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And there came out a fire from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and consumed the two hundred and fifty men that offered incense. <hi type="super">36</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">37</hi> Speak unto Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest, that he take up the censers out of the burning, and scatter thou the fire yonder; for they are hallowed. <hi type="super">38</hi> The censers of these sinners against their own souls, let them make them broad plates <hi type="italic">for</hi> a covering of the altar: for they offered them before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , therefore they are hallowed: and they shall be a sign unto the children of Israel. <hi type="super">39</hi> And Eleazar the priest took the brazen censers, wherewith they that were burnt had offered; and they were made broad <hi type="italic">plates for</hi> a covering of the altar: <hi type="super">40</hi> <hi type="italic">To be</hi> a memorial unto the children of Israel, that no stranger, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> not of the seed of Aaron, come near to offer incense before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that he be not as Korah, and as his company: as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said to him by the hand of Moses. <div eID="gen3018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3019" type="x-p"/> We must now look back to the door of the tabernacle, where we left the pretenders to the priesthood with their censers in their hands ready to offer incense; and here we find, <div eID="gen3019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3020" type="x-p"/> I. Vengeance taken on them, <reference osisRef="Num.16.35">v. 35</reference>. It is probable that when the earth opened in the camp to swallow up Dathan and Abiram <hi type="italic">a fire went out from the Lord and consumed the 250 men that offered incense,</hi> while Aaron that stood with them was preserved alive. This punishment was not indeed so new a thing as the former, for Nadab and Abihu thus died; but it was not less strange or dreadful, and in it it appeared, 1. That <hi type="italic">our God is a consuming fire.</hi> Is thunder a sensible indication of the terror of his voice? Lightning is also the power of his hand. We must see in this his fiery indignation which devours the adversaries, and infer from it what a fearful thing it is to <hi type="italic">fall into the hands of the living God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27-Heb.10.31">Heb. x. 27-31</reference>. 2. That it is at our peril if we meddle with that which does not belong to us. God is jealous of the honour of his own institutions, and will not have them invaded. It is most probable that Korah himself was consumed with those 250 that presumed to offer incense; for the priesthood was the thing he aimed at, and therefore we have reason to think that he would not quit his post at the door of the tabernacle. But, behold, those are made sacrifices to the justice of God who flattered themselves with the hopes of being priests. Had they been content with their office as Levites, which was sacred and honourable, and better than they deserved, they might have lived and died with joy and reputation; but, like the angels that sinned, <hi type="italic">leaving their first estate,</hi> and aiming at the honours that were not appointed them, they were thrust down to <hi type="italic">Hades,</hi> their censers struck out of their hands, and their breath out of their bodies, by a burning which typified <hi type="italic">the vengeance of eternal fire.</hi> <div eID="gen3020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3021" type="x-p"/> II. Care is taken to perpetuate the remembrance of this vengeance. No mention is made of the taking up of their carcases: the scripture leaves them as dung upon the face of the earth; but orders are given about their censers, 1. That they be secured, because they are hallowed. Eleazar is charged with this, <reference osisRef="Num.16.37">v. 37</reference>. Those invaders of the priesthood had proceeded so far, by the divine patience and submission, as to kindle their incense with fire from off the altar, which they were suffered to use by way of experiment: but, as soon as they had kindled their fire, God kindled another, which put a fatal final period to their pretensions; now Eleazar is ordered to scatter the fire, with the incense that was kindled with it, in some unclean place without the camp, to signify God's abhorrence of their offering as a polluted thing: <hi type="italic">The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord.</hi> But he is to gather up the censers out of the mingled burning, God's fire and theirs, because <hi type="italic">they are hallowed.</hi> Having been once put to a holy use, and that by God's own order (though only for trial), they must not return to common service; so some understand it: rather, <hi type="italic">they are devoted,</hi> they are an anathema; and therefore, as all devoted things, they must be made some way or other serviceable to the glory of God. 2. That they be used in the service of the sanctuary, not as censers, which would rather have put honour upon the usurpers whose disgrace was intended; nor was there occasion for brazen censers, the golden altar was served with golden ones; but they must be beaten into <hi type="italic">broad plates for a covering of the brazen altar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.38-Num.16.40">v. 38-40</reference>. These pretenders thought to have ruined the altar, by laying the priesthood in common again; but to show that Aaron's office was so far from being shaken by their impotent malice that it was rather confirmed by it, their censers, which offered to rival his, were used both for the adorning and for the preserving of the altar at which he ministered. Yet this was not all; this covering of the altar must be a <hi type="italic">memorial to the children of Israel,</hi> throughout their generations, of this great event. Though there was so much in it astonishing, and though Moses was to record it in his history, yet there was danger of its being forgotten in process of time; impressions that seem deep are not always durable; therefore it was necessary to appoint this record of the judgment, that the Levites who attended this altar, and had their inferior services appointed them, might learn to keep within their bounds, and be afraid of transgressing them, lest they should be made like Korah and his company, who were Levites, and would have been priests. These censers were preserved <hi type="italic">in terrorem,</hi> that others might hear and fear, and do no more presumptuously. Thus God has provided that his wonderful works, both in mercy and judgment, should be had in everlasting remembrance, that the end of them may be answered, and they may serve for instruction and admonition to those <hi type="italic">on whom the ends of the world are come.</hi>
entries.37efe56b1fdaaf528ea5e4d07dd3c81e3d83b1ea: <div eID="gen3021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> But on the morrow all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, Ye have killed the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">42</hi> And it came to pass, when the congregation was gathered against Moses and against Aaron, that they looked toward the tabernacle of the congregation: and, behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> appeared. <hi type="super">43</hi> And Moses and Aaron came before the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">44</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, 45 Get you up from among this congregation, that I may consume them as in a moment. And they fell upon their faces. <hi type="super">46</hi> And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; the plague is begun. <hi type="super">47</hi> And Aaron took as Moses commanded, and ran into the midst of the congregation; and, behold, the plague was begun among the people: and he put on incense, and made an atonement for the people. <hi type="super">48</hi> And he stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed. <hi type="super">49</hi> Now they that died in the plague were fourteen thousand and seven hundred, beside them that died about the matter of Korah. <hi type="super">50</hi> And Aaron returned unto Moses unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation: and the plague was stayed. <div eID="gen3022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3023" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A new rebellion raised the very next day against Moses and Aaron. Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and wonder, O earth! Was there ever such an instance of the incurable corruption of sinners? <hi type="italic">On the morrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.41">v. 41</reference>) the body of the people mutinied. 1. Though they were so lately terrified by the sight of the punishment of the rebels. The shrieks of those sinking sinners, those sinners against their own souls, were yet sounding in their ears, the smell of the fire yet remained, and the gaping earth was scarcely thoroughly closed, and yet the same sins were re-acted and all these warnings slighted. 2. Though they were so lately saved from sharing in the same punishment, and the survivors were <hi type="italic">as brands plucked out of the burning,</hi> yet they fly in the face of Moses and Aaron, to whose intercession they owed their preservation. Their charge runs very high: <hi type="italic">You have killed the people of the Lord.</hi> Could any thing have been said more unjustly and maliciously? They canonize the rebels, calling those the people of the Lord who died in arms against him. They stigmatize divine justice itself. It was plain enough that Moses and Aaron had no hand in their death (they did what they could to save them), so that in charging them with murder they did in effect charge God himself with it. The continued obstinacy of this people, notwithstanding the terrors of God's law as it was given on Mount Sinai, and the terrors of his judgments as they were here executed on the disobedient, shows how necessary the grace of God is to the effectual change of men's hearts and lives, without which the most likely means will never attain the end. Love will do what fear could not. <div eID="gen3023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3024" type="x-p"/> II. God's speedy appearance against the rebels. When they had <hi type="italic">gathered against Moses and Aaron,</hi> perhaps with a design to depose or murder them, they <hi type="italic">looked towards the tabernacle,</hi> as if their misgiving consciences expected some frowns thence, and, <hi type="italic">behold, the glory of the Lord appeared</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.16.42">v. 42</reference>), for the protection of his servants, and the confusion of his and their accusers and adversaries. Moses and Aaron thereupon came before the tabernacle, partly for their own safety (there they took sanctuary from the strife of tongues, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">xxxi. 20</reference>), and partly for advice, to know what was the mind of God upon this occasion, <reference osisRef="Num.16.43">v. 43</reference>. Justice hereupon declares that they deserve to be <hi type="italic">consumed in a moment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.16.45">v. 45</reference>. Why should those live another day who hate to be reformed, and whose rebellions are their daily practices? Let just vengeance take place and do its work, and the trouble will soon be over; only Moses and Aaron must first be secured. <div eID="gen3024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3025" type="x-p"/> III. The intercession which Moses and Aaron made for them. Though they had as much reason, one would think, as Elias had to make intercession against Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.2">Rom. xi. 2</reference>), yet they forgive and forget the indignities offered them, and are the best friends their enemies have. 1. They both <hi type="italic">fell on their faces,</hi> humbly to intercede with God for mercy, knowing how great the provocation was. This they had done several times before, upon similar occasions; and, though the people had basely requited them for it, yet, God having graciously accepted them, they still have recourse to the same method. This is praying always. 2. Moses, perceiving that the <hi type="italic">plague had begun in the congregation</hi> of the rebels (that is, that body of them which was gathered against Moses), sent Aaron by an act of his priestly office to make atonement for them, <reference osisRef="Num.16.46">v. 46</reference>. And Aaron readily went and burned incense between the living and the dead, not to purify the infected air, but to pacify an offended God, and so stayed the progress of the judgment. By this it appeared, (1.) That Aaron was a very good man, and a man that had a true love for the children of his people, though they hated and envied him. Though God was now avenging his quarrel and pleading the cause of his priesthood, yet he interposes to turn away God's wrath. Nay, forgetting his age and gravity, he ran into the midst of the congregation to help them. He did not say, "Let them smart awhile, and then, when I come, I shall be the more welcome;" but, as one tender of the life of every Israelite, he makes all possible speed into the gap at which death was entering. Moses and Aaron, who had been charged with killing the people of the Lord, might justly have upbraided them now; could they expect those to be their saviours whom they had so invidiously called their murderers? But those good men have taught us here by their example not to be sullen towards those that are peevish with us, nor to take the advantage which men give us by their provoking language to deny them any real kindness which it is in the power of our hands to do them. We must render good for evil. (2.) That Aaron was a very bold man—bold to venture into the midst of an enraged rabble that were gathered together against him, and who, for aught he knew, might be the more exasperated by the plague that had begun—bold to venture into the midst of the infection, where the arrows of death flew thickest, and hundreds, nay thousands, were falling on the right hand and on the left. To save their lives he put his own into his hand, not counting it dear to him, so that he might but fulfil his ministry. (3.) That Aaron was a man of God, and <hi type="italic">ordained for men, in things pertaining to God.</hi> His call to the priesthood was hereby abundantly confirmed and set above all contradiction; God had not only saved his life when the intruders were cut off, but now made him an instrument for saving Israel. Compare the censer of Aaron here with the <hi type="italic">censers of those sinners against their own souls.</hi> Those provoked God's anger, this pacified it; those destroyed men's lives, this saved them; no room therefore is left to doubt of Aaron's call to the priesthood. Note, Those make out the best title to public honours that lay out themselves the most for public good and obtain mercy of the Lord to be faithful and useful. If any man will be great, let him make himself the servant of all. (4.) That Aaron was a type of Christ, who came into the world to make an atonement for sin and to turn away the wrath of God from us, and who, by his mediation and intercession, <hi type="italic">stands between the living and the dead,</hi> to secure his chosen Israel to himself, and save them out of the midst of a world infected with sin and the curse. <div eID="gen3025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3026" type="x-p"/> IV. The result and issue of the whole matter. 1. God's justice was glorified in the death of some. Great execution the sword of the Lord did in a very little time. Though Aaron made all the haste he could, yet, before he could reach his post of service, there were 14,700 men laid dead upon the spot, <reference osisRef="Num.16.49">v. 49</reference>. There were but few comparatively that died about the matter of Korah, the ring-leaders only were made examples; but, the people not being led to repentance by the patience and forbearance of God with them, justice is not now so sparing of the blood of Israelites. They complained of the death of a few hundreds as an unmerciful slaughter made among the <hi type="italic">people of the Lord,</hi> but here God silences that complaint by the slaughter of many thousands. Note, Those that quarrel with less judgments prepare greater for themselves; for when God judges he will overcome. 2. His mercy was glorified in the preservation of the rest. God showed them what he could do by his power, and what he might do in justice, but then showed them what he would do in his love and pity: he would, notwithstanding all this, preserve them a people to himself in and by a mediator. The cloud of Aaron's incense coming from his hand stayed the plague. Note, It is much for the glory of God's goodness that many a time even in wrath he remembers mercy. And, even when judgments have been begun, prayer puts a stop to them; so ready is he to forgive, and so little pleasure does he take in the death of sinners.  <chapter eID="Num.16"/> <div eID="gen3026" type="x-p"/>

entries.20196ca159e95d26ef188aa6f395e997547d899c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1407"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.16.1-Num.16.30">Nu 16:1-30</reference>. The Rebellion of Korah.</title> <div sID="gen1898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1407"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Now Korah, the son of Izhar--</hi>Izhar, brother of Amram (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.18">Ex 6:18</reference>), was the second son of Kohath, and for some reason unrecorded he had been supplanted by a descendant of the fourth son of Kohath, who was appointed prince or chief of the Kohathites (<reference osisRef="Num.3.30">Nu 3:30</reference>). Discontent with the preferment over him of a younger relative was probably the originating cause of this seditious movement on the part of Korah.<div eID="gen1898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Dathan and Abiram, ... and On--</hi>These were confederate leaders in the rebellion, but On seems to have afterwards withdrawn from the conspiracy [compare <reference osisRef="Num.16.12">Nu 16:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.25">24, 25</reference>, 27; <reference osisRef="Num.26.9">26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">De 11:6</reference>; Psa 106:17].<div eID="gen1899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took men--</hi>The latter mentioned individuals, being all sons of Reuben, the eldest of Jacob's family, had been stimulated to this insurrection on the pretext that Moses had, by an arbitrary arrangement, taken away the right of primogeniture, which had vested the hereditary dignity of the priesthood in the first-born of every family, with a view of transferring the hereditary exercise of the sacred functions to a particular branch of his own house; and that this gross instance of partiality to his own relations, to the permanent detriment of others, was a sufficient ground for refusing allegiance to his government. In addition to this grievance, another cause of jealousy and dissatisfaction that rankled in the breasts of the Reubenites was the advancement of Judah to the leadership among the tribes. These malcontents had been incited by the artful representations of Korah (Jude 11), with whom the position of their camp on the south side afforded them facilities of frequent intercourse. In addition to his feeling of personal wrongs, Korah participated in their desire (if he did not originate the attempt) to recover their lost rights of primogeniture. When the conspiracy was ripe, they openly and boldly declared its object, and at the head of two hundred fifty princes, charged Moses with an ambitious and unwarrantable usurpation of authority, especially in the appropriation of the priesthood, for they disputed the claim of Aaron also to pre-eminence [Nu 16:3]. <div eID="gen1900" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d4b1ef34f58f9ae5533396a8c35550468c925ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1408"/><div sID="gen1901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1408"/><hi type="bold">3. they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron--</hi>The assemblage seems to have been composed of the whole band of conspirators; and they grounded their complaint on the fact that the whole people, being separated to the divine service (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>), were equally qualified to present offerings on the altar, and that God, being graciously, present among them by the tabernacle and the cloud, evinced His readiness to receive sacrifices from the hand of any others as well as from theirs. <div eID="gen1901" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6cd24cf6f5fdad42f0e0c4ed218064474362c6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1409"/><div sID="gen1902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1409"/><hi type="bold">4. when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face--</hi>This attitude of prostration indicated not only his humble and earnest desire that God would interpose to free him from the false and odious imputation, but also his strong sense of the daring sin involved in this proceeding. Whatever feelings may be entertained respecting Aaron, who had formerly headed a sedition himself [Nu 12:1], it is impossible not to sympathize with Moses in this difficult emergency. But he was a devout man, and the prudential course he adopted was probably the dictate of that heavenly wisdom with which, in answer to his prayers, he was endowed. <div eID="gen1902" type="x-p"/>
entries.366aa2057712defb68d1082c327a9916df02be07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1410"/><div sID="gen1903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1410"/><hi type="bold">5-11. he spake unto Korah and unto all his company--</hi>They were first addressed, not only because they were a party headed by his own cousin and Moses might hope to have more influence in that quarter, but because they were stationed near the tabernacle; and especially because an expostulation was the more weighty coming from him who was a Levite himself, and who was excluded along with his family from the priesthood. But to bring the matter to an issue, he proposed a test which would afford a decisive evidence of the divine appointment.<div eID="gen1903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Even to-morrow--</hi>literally, "in the morning," the usual time of meeting in the East for the settlement of public affairs.<div eID="gen1904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord will show who are his, ... even him whom he hath chosen will he cause to come near unto him--</hi>that is, will bear attestation to his ministry by some visible or miraculous token of His approval. <div eID="gen1905" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9b9539a1526de6b85c535312c255892a631b473: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1412"/><div sID="gen1907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1412"/><hi type="bold">12-14. Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram--</hi>in a separate interview, the ground of their mutiny being different; for while Korah murmured against the exclusive appropriation of the priesthood to Aaron and his family, they were opposed to the supremacy of Moses in civil power. They refused to obey the summons; and their refusal was grounded on the plausible pretext that their stay in the desert was prolonged for some secret and selfish purposes of the leader, who was conducting them like blind men wherever it suited him. <div eID="gen1907" type="x-p"/>
entries.8091c6ac14112ebe324d28cb67885507eebcec10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1413"/><div sID="gen1908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1413"/><hi type="bold">15. Moses was very wroth--</hi>Though the meekest of all men [Nu 12:3], he could not restrain his indignation at these unjust and groundless charges; and the highly excited state of his feeling was evinced by the utterance of a brief exclamation in the mixed form of a prayer and an impassioned assertion of his integrity. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>).<div eID="gen1908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said unto the Lord, Respect not thou their offering--</hi>He calls it their offering, because, though it was to be offered by Korah and his Levitical associates, it was the united appeal of all the mutineers for deciding the contested claims of Moses and Aaron. <div eID="gen1909" type="x-p"/>
entries.15015f8c8a8e33c43a02f7ba42642ed5a3143f08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1414"/><div sID="gen1910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1414"/><hi type="bold">16-18. Moses said unto Korah, Be thou and all thy company before the Lord--</hi>that is, at "the door of the tabernacle" (<reference osisRef="Num.16.18">Nu 16:18</reference>), that the assembled people might witness the experiment and be properly impressed by the issue. <div eID="gen1910" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8963911873d590ff81c1f3570c7e09760f09ac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1416"/><div sID="gen1912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1416"/><hi type="bold">20-21. the Lord spake unto Moses and Aaron, saying, Separate yourselves from among this congregation--</hi>Curiosity to witness the exciting spectacle attracted a vast concourse of the people, and it would seem that the popular mind had been incited to evil by the clamors of the mutineers against Moses and Aaron. There was something in their behavior very offensive to God; for after His glory had appeared--as at the installation of Aaron (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.23">Le 9:23</reference>), so now for his confirmation in the sacred office--He bade Moses and Aaron withdraw from the assembly "that He might consume them in a moment." <div eID="gen1912" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0c12530ad0e6e1aa77b7d3dd83732f41762c26f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1417"/><div sID="gen1913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1417"/><hi type="bold">22. they fell upon their faces, and said, O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh--</hi>The benevolent importunity of their prayer was the more remarkable that the intercession was made for their enemies. <div eID="gen1913" type="x-p"/>
entries.c12e21d99b48dfb209bc0e975790f78ebf1765f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1418"/><div sID="gen1914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1418"/><hi type="bold">24-26. Speak unto the congregation, ... Get you up from about the tabernacle--</hi>Moses was attended in the execution of this mission by the elders. The united and urgent entreaties of so many dignified personages produced the desired effect of convincing the people of their crime, and of withdrawing them from the company of men who were doomed to destruction, lest, being partakers of their sins, they should perish along with them. <div eID="gen1914" type="x-p"/>
entries.e954617139d1f54e3ae353dab2f6cc68615b0c6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1419"/><div sID="gen1915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1419"/><hi type="bold">27. the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram--</hi>Korah being a Kohathite, his tent could not have been in the Reubenite camp, and it does not appear that he himself was on the spot where Dathan and Abiram stood with their families. Their attitude of defiance indicated their daring and impenitent character, equally regardless of God and man. <div eID="gen1915" type="x-p"/>
entries.1662f7014e531b53ab1ab083c480577f79af5d7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1420"/><div sID="gen1916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1420"/><hi type="bold">28-34. Moses said, Hereby ye shall know that the Lord hath sent me to do all these works--</hi>The awful catastrophe of the earthquake which, as predicted by Moses, swallowed up those impious rebels in a living tomb, gave the divine attestation to the mission of Moses and struck the spectators with solemn awe. <div eID="gen1916" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a9596b6bb7e4884a85912127c42f420838c4cf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1421"/><div sID="gen1917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1421"/><hi type="bold">35. there came out a fire from the Lord--</hi>that is, from the cloud. This seems to describe the destruction of Korah and those Levites who with him aspired to the functions of the priesthood. (See <reference osisRef="Num.26.11">Nu 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.26.58">58</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.22">1Ch 6:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.37">37</reference>). <div eID="gen1917" type="x-p"/>
